## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.77632.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.77632.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Measurements of damage and repair in aging mice and humans reveals that robustness and resilience decrease with age, operate over broad timescales, and are affected differently by interventions" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 4 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Carlos Isales as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Konstantin Arbeev (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1. A key assumption is that an increase in FI is equivalent to a rise in damage, but this relationship is unknown and may ignore a number of important biological processes – including the dynamic interplay between both damage, compensatory processes/feedback, and protection/fitness. There is lingering concern that this may be over-conceptualized, and the true relationship between frailty index and damage is unknown. This should be addressed in the manuscript rationale. Language in discussion and conclusions should be tempered.

2. Additionally, 'repair' assumes a biological process to restore homeostasis, but in this manuscript refers to a switch from out-of-range to a return to in-range for variables and cut-points that are not defined in the manuscript. The issue of measurement error in individual components that switch from out-of-range to in-range or vice versa needs to be addressed. Variables and cutpoints must be detailed. Authors should also distinguish biological processes from mechanical definitions in rationale and discussion.

3. Some variables may represent irreversible processes of deterioration (e.g. loss of whiskers, kyphosis, palpable/visible tumor, etc.), while others may be more dynamic or have cutpoints with unknown validity for in vs out of range. It is anticipated that only a subset of those queried contributes to 'repair' while others irreversibly increase over time. This would challenge the validity of 'repair' models (and interpretation of Figure 5). As above, please include details on specific variables and their cutpoints. Please indicate which of these variables change dynamically over time – with evidence of both 'deficit' and 'repair' – versus those that are irreparable by definition or thresholds.

4. Additional conceptual issues are present in mouse models given typically shorter time scales and acute stress stimulus – in addition to the issues above. Most reviewers have requested additional details to support assumptions made in mouse models.

5. Detailed total follow-up time/time-course in both animal and human data is needed. For example, statistics on total follow-up times in human data. This is important for relative time courses across species and how many times deficits can be damaged/repaired within a given time or relative period of life.

6. Concern over the impact of selection bias/survivor bias in models (especially mice). Please address in the model and discussion.

7. Abstract requires clarity. Data, tests performed, and specific results should be presented as appropriate.

8. Please address specific recommendations and editorial suggestions made by each reviewer below.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I commend the authors for their efforts. The modeling of longitudinal data is an important area in aging that needs more attention. I also like the approach at a conceptual level and think the stratification of resilience vs robustness could be quite valuable. I appreciate the idea of making models that are generalizable and think the approach is most appropriate for the human data, but I think more attention needs to be paid to the technical and biological aspects of the variables being modeled for the mouse data.

General comments:

The mouse frailty index is a very useful tool for efficiently measuring the organismal state in large cohorts. A tradeoff for quickly measuring a broad range of health domains is that the individual measurements are low resolution and involve inherent subjectivity (which may be considered measurement error). It is very important to keep this in mind when using individual scores from the index. Some transitions are due to random measurement error and I believe this is especially likely with decreases (or 'resilience' transitions).

While I find the 'robustness' modeling quite interesting, I am skeptical as to how valid the 'resilience' modeling is. The first reason for this is that I do not believe many of the deficits in the mouse index are reversible under normal physiologic conditions. For example, it is exceptionally unlikely for a palpable/visible tumor to resolve in an aged mouse, thus any reversal that was observed must be due to random measurement error. I would conservatively estimate that the following components are not truly reversible in the contexts in which they were studied here: alopecia, loss of fur color, loss of whiskers, tumors, kyphosis, hearing loss, cataracts, corneal capacity, vision loss, rectal prolapse, genital prolapse.

When used as a sum of its components, the mouse frailty index is highly robust to these measurement errors as demonstrated many times in the literature. However, breaking apart the index into its components compromises this robustness, and I am not aware of literature which has validated the use of individual components of the index. How do the authors account for the measurement error which is inherent to the individual components of the mouse frailty index, and how might this error affect their models? I would be particularly concerned with how this would affect the models in figure 5.

Additionally, the authors state that "the observed damage is thought to occur due to natural stochastic transitions." I do not necessarily agree with that characterization for many of the pathologies measured here. For example, I would not consider vision loss a stochastic transition but rather a gradual degenerative process. Stochasticity involves when it crosses a threshold that can be measured/detected by the researcher. The authors state the following assumption: "We assume these time intervals are small so that we use constant rates within each time-interval to approximate these integrals." Small is subjective and the time intervals are up to 2 months which is 7-10% of a mouse lifespan. Can the authors justify this assumption and/or discuss the implications of such an assumption to their models? The time scale should also be considered in the context of the specific measurements being taken.

My final high-level comment regards selection bias. As these studies progress and individuals die, the study population drastically changes. How do the authors' models account for this selection bias? Can the results of the modelling tell us anything about the nature of the populations as selection occurs? And finally, would there be value in performing this modeling as a function of "biological age" (ie. time to death) versus chronological age?

Specific comments:

The authors should specify which packages and versions were used for the development of their models. When I ran some of the scripts from Github they threw pandas warnings, leading me to suspect that I am not using the development versions. This is important if the authors expect future use of their models. I would encourage the authors to include package information both in the manuscript and on the Github.

I would recommend the authors be specific when describing their results. Many complex models and statistical tests are generated and it sometimes is unclear what is being referred to. For example, in the section "The acceleration of damage accumulation…" the statement "In mice, this is seen in every dataset and is significant at the indicated ages" is unclear what statistical test is being referred to. I would also recommend the authors be more precise in their result descriptions. For example, in the section "Interventions modify damage…" the statement "This curvature is strongly reduced…" is subjective and would be better supported by a description of specific statistical results.

The authors should be careful with the language used regarding wealth in the human dataset. Wealth is not an intervention. And wealth per se does not influence frailty as worded in methods. In these data wealth is a variable which is often associated with health outcomes including frailty.

In discussion: "…where female live longer but have higher FI scores than males." Female humans live longer but female B6 mice usually live shorter.

The citation the authors use for ELSA points to the database. PMID 23143611 also needs to be cited where the study and data collection procedures are described. It also seems like an omission to not cite PMID 31665163 which explores the relationship between various factors, including wealth, and frailty in the same dataset. I would also recommend the authors include a supplemental table with the specific mouse measurements and human questionnaire items that comprise the respective frailty indices.

The authors should provide more detail on the human frailty variables in the methods. I am assuming the binary responses to questions HEADLA and HEADLB were used, but this should be clarified/explicitly stated in the methods.

Comments on mouse pre-processing methods: In the mouse frailty index, 29 out of 31 parameters are measured on a [0, 0.5, 1] scale, with only weight and temperature using [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1] scale, and it looks to me like the Schultz dataset still used [0, 0.5, 1] for these variables. So I don't find the statement "a single repair or damage transition can be interpreted as taking a step of size 0.25 on the fractional deficit scale" to be accurate because 29 out of 31 parameters only have the resolution to move in 0.5 unit increments.

Page 5: Authors state that "in each of the datasets, there is a strong decrease in repair rates and increase in damage rates with age (except in mouse dataset 2 for damage rates)." This doesn't seem to be the case for repair rates in humans entering ELSA study at age 50-70 (CI for p cross 0).

I am also somewhat unclear about the values for the rates in figure 2. In figure S2-1 the authors show that the model fits the data reasonably well. However, when looking at the rates in figure 2, the repair rates appear to be consistently higher than the damage rates. For example, in the Keller dataset males at 22 months, as frailty is consistently increasing, the modeled repair rate appears to be nearly double the modelled damage rate. Overall, the comparative magnitudes of the rates don't seem consistent with the mouse data, where there it is relatively rare to see a "population level" reduction in frailty at a subsequent timepoint (tends to stay the same or increase over time as shown in Figure 2S-2). Same comment for figure 4S2 human data.

Figure S2-1. It is hard to see the bars of the histogram in comparison to the dots. I would recommend making the dots smaller. Quantifying and plotting the deviation of observed vs posterior samples may also make interpretation easier.

The repair rate in the human 70-80 data (2d) appears to have a negative curvature, but this doesn't seem to be reflected in the second derivative plot (3e, teal line centered on zero).

I find the models in figure 5 somewhat difficult to interpret considering the extensive censoring that is occurring. Could the authors attempt a more 'plain language' interpretation of these curves considering the censoring? It seems like the interpretation would be that at 3 months after damage there is only a 75% probability of that damage being repaired? Also, could the authors interpret the drastic reduction in probability occurring in both damage and repair of the Schultz data at ~3 months?

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

I find the result on sex differences in effects of interventions on robustness and resilience very interesting so consider mentioning this in the abstract.

I would like to see more discussion on why deficits can be repaired, especially for some deficits which may seem to represent irreversible processes of deterioration. One example that is not trivial for me to understand (as I am not a specialist in mice) is the repair of the deficit "loss of whiskers." Do they just grow up again after a while? If they do, what constitutes the event of repair (just when they start growing again or when they are fully grown, assuming there is a measure for this)?

Some statistics on the total follow-up times in human data would be helpful. It can help put the estimates of repair/damage scales in the context to provide insight on how many times the deficit can potentially be damaged/repaired in the time period of data collection.

As you indicated in Methods, "The individuals selected from ELSA with wealth data do not have mortality data available, simplifying the model from the joint model used above for mice." In Results, you wrote, "This is a joint longitudinal-survival model, which couples the damage and repair rates together with mortality." This narrative should be changed then to reflect the fact that the joint model was only used in mice data.

Some readers may not be familiar with Bayesian methods so it would help provide in Methods some discussion on the selection of priors – is this a convenience/traditional choice or some other reasons? Also, some narrative on the sensitivity of results to a different choice of priors would be helpful, in my view.

results.result: The authors develop a novel method to measure damage and repair rates from longitudinal binary health deficit data. Damage rates represent the probability of acquiring a new deficit per unit time, and repair rates represent the probability of repairing a deficit per unit time. These aggregate rates are whole organism-level measures of robustness (resistance to damage) and resilience (ability to repair).
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16 describe the methodological framework clearly and consistently. The approach is illustrated in Figure 1 and mathematically defined in the Methods section. The definitions are internally consistent and the mathematical relationships are sound.

results.result: Both mice and humans exhibit decreasing repair rates (resilience) and increasing damage rates (robustness decline) with age, which together contribute to the increasing Frailty Index with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C19-C21, and C51 are strongly supported by data in Figure 2 showing consistent age-dependent trends across three mouse datasets and human data. Spearman correlations are provided with credible intervals, and posterior predictive checks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) demonstrate good model quality.

results.result: Declining robustness (increasing damage rates) has a greater effect than declining resilience (decreasing repair rates) on both the acceleration of Frailty Index accumulation and survival. Damage rates have approximately twice the effect on FI curvature and show larger hazard ratios for death compared to repair rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C25, C30-C31, and C53-C54 are supported by curvature analysis in Figure 3 and hazard ratio analysis in Figure 2e-g. The statistical significance is demonstrated through credible intervals, and the finding is consistent across multiple mouse datasets. The joint longitudinal-survival modeling approach appropriately accounts for the relationship between rates and mortality.

results.result: The Frailty Index exhibits positive curvature (acceleration) with age. Both decreasing robustness and resilience contribute to this acceleration, addressing a previously unknown question about the origin of this curvature.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 and C52 are supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3. The curvature decomposition analysis (Equation 22 in Methods) provides a rigorous mathematical framework for separating the contributions of damage and repair processes to FI acceleration.

results.result: Enalapril and voluntary exercise interventions in mice affect both damage and repair rates in age- and sex-dependent manners. Exercise strongly reduces FI curvature and shows sex-specific effects: it stops the decline in repair rates for females but not males, and stops the increase in damage rates for males but not females.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C32-C38, and C66 are supported by intervention data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The sex-specific effects are clearly demonstrated with credible intervals. However, the mechanisms underlying these differential effects are not explored, and sample sizes for some intervention groups are relatively small (e.g., 6 male mice in dataset 2).

results.result: In humans, household wealth is positively correlated with repair rates and negatively correlated with damage rates, with stronger effects at younger ages. Higher wealth is associated with lower Frailty Index.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by data in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. However, the authors acknowledge potential confounding by recruitment effects (C43), and wealth is correlational rather than interventional. The lack of mortality data for humans limits the ability to assess survival effects.

results.result: Both damage and repair processes operate over a broad range of timescales, from the shortest measurement intervals to organismal lifetimes. Different health attributes exhibit different recovery and damage timescales, and repair can occur long after the original damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C44-C46, C81-C82 are supported by state-survival curves in Figure 5 and exponential timescale analysis in Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2. The interval-censored survival modeling approach is appropriate for the data structure. However, the authors acknowledge that fast dynamics shorter than measurement intervals may be missed (C60).

results.result: Interventions show limited effects on damage and repair timescales in mice, with exercise slightly accelerating repair in male mice. In humans, household wealth shows strong sex-specific effects on timescales in females but not males, particularly for damage timescales (robustness).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by Figure 5b-e with generalized log-rank tests. The sex-specific effects in humans are statistically significant. However, the limited effects in mice may reflect insufficient statistical power or the need to stratify by time of damage/repair occurrence.

results.result: Females exhibit higher Frailty Index scores than males in both mice and humans. While age effects on damage and repair are qualitatively similar between sexes, interventions show sex-specific effects: enalapril has stronger effects in female mice, and exercise shows opposite effects on repair rates (stops decline in females) versus damage rates (stops increase in males).
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C71-C76 are supported by data throughout Figure 2, Figure 4, and supplementary figures. The sex differences are consistent with prior literature (C22 cites previous work). However, the mechanisms underlying sex-specific intervention effects are not explored, and sample sizes for some sex-intervention combinations are small.

results.result: Almost all mouse health deficits used in the study have been previously shown to reverse either spontaneously or through interventions. Only a few deficits (cataracts, tumours, diarrhea, prolapses) rarely or never repair. Most deficits in the mouse frailty index can be reversed or repaired.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 and C83-C85 are supported by Supplementary file 1 with literature references and by Figure 5—figure supplement 4 showing repair counts per deficit. This addresses a potential concern about whether the observed 'repair' represents true biological reversal versus measurement error.

results.result: The authors suggest that interventions targeting robustness may be more effective than those targeting resilience, particularly at older ages. They propose that interventions could be improved by targeting an appropriate balance of damage and repair processes in age- and sex-dependent manners.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 and C67-C70 are speculative predictions and suggestions based on the findings (marked as SPECULATION and INFERENCE). While the underlying data about robustness having stronger effects is supported, these forward-looking recommendations require experimental validation through targeted intervention studies.

results.result: Both decreasing robustness and decreasing resilience are important processes underlying the increasing accumulation of health-related deficits with age. The universally observed accelerating accumulation of deficits must be reflected in increasing damage rates, decreasing repair rates, or both.
results.evaluation: Claims C55 and C78 synthesize the main findings and are supported by the comprehensive data across figures. C78 represents a logical inference from the mathematical relationship between rates and FI (Equation 18). This contrasts with prior literature focus on resilience alone (C55 cites Ukraintseva et al., 2021).

results.result: The study measures damage and repair from natural aging processes rather than applied stressors, likely representing intrinsic resilience and robustness. The binarized variable approach allows estimation of both resilience and robustness using similar methods on the same data, unlike previous work that modeled total deficit counts without separating damage and repair.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 describe methodological context and advantages. These are well-supported by citations to prior work and clear explanation of the novel contribution. The comparison to previous approaches (C59) is appropriately referenced.

results.result: The method has limitations: it may miss fast dynamics shorter than measurement intervals, measurements represent net damage/repair between timepoints, and the relationship to continuous health attributes is unknown. Measurement errors could contribute to rates but presumably not age-dependently, and sensitivity analysis shows no qualitative changes when pruning putative errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 honestly acknowledge methodological limitations. The sensitivity analysis (C65, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) demonstrates robustness to potential measurement errors. The acknowledgment of limitations is appropriate and well-reasoned.

results.result: The mechanisms coupling damage and repair processes during aging remain unknown. The authors speculate that spontaneous repair occurs through the same pathways targeted by interventions, likely involving molecular/cellular pillars of aging. For the specific interventions studied, prior work suggests effects are mediated through chronic inflammation.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 identify important open questions supported by citations. Claims C86-C87 are explicitly speculative. C88 is supported by citations to prior mechanistic work on enalapril and exercise. These represent appropriate discussion of mechanisms and future directions but lack direct experimental evidence in the current study.

results.result: The study uses three mouse datasets with different assessment frequencies and interventions (enalapril, exercise), and human data from ELSA. The mouse clinical frailty index involves 31 (or 29) non-invasive health measures, and the human FI uses 23 ADL/IADL items. A joint longitudinal-survival modeling framework is used for mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C99 and C101 describe the experimental design and data sources. These are clearly documented with appropriate citations to the original data sources. The methods are described in sufficient detail for the statistical modeling approach.

results.result: Traditional frailty measures (FI, Frailty Phenotype) do not separate dynamic damage and repair processes but are associated with adverse outcomes. Prior literature has focused on resilience decline with age, while robustness decline is less studied. Organismal-scale damage may exhibit distinct behavior from cellular/molecular damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C11 provide literature context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the study by identifying gaps in current approaches and knowledge. The citations are to established work in the field.

results.result: As an organism ages, its health-state is determined by a balance between the processes of damage and repair.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is a foundational conceptual statement that frames the entire study. While it is a general principle rather than a specific finding, it is well-supported by the overall results demonstrating that both damage and repair processes contribute to health state evolution.

results.result: Recent work in humans has shown that FI damage is more associated with mortality than FI repair, consistent with the findings in mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 cites recent work (Shi et al., 2021) that corroborates the mouse findings in humans. This provides external validation for the relative importance of damage versus repair for mortality, though the authors did not have mortality data for their human cohort.

results.result: The study reports that robustness (resistance to damage) and resilience (ability to repair) both decrease with age in mice and humans, as evidenced by increasing damage rates and decreasing repair rates with age across multiple datasets (Figure 2). These changes contribute to the accelerating accumulation of frailty index deficits observed with aging.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised fundamental concerns about the conceptual framework, noting that 'the relationship between frailty index and damage is unknown and may ignore important biological processes' (Essential Revision 1). They also questioned whether observed 'repair' transitions represent true biological repair or measurement error, particularly for deficits that may be irreversible (Essential Revision 2-3, Reviewer #1). While reviewers acknowledged the modeling approach, they expressed skepticism about the validity of resilience modeling given measurement error and the reversibility of individual frailty index components.

results.result: The study claims that declining robustness (increasing damage rates) has a greater effect than declining resilience (decreasing repair rates) on both the acceleration of frailty index accumulation with age (approximately twice as large based on curvature analysis in Figure 3) and on mortality risk (larger hazard ratios in Figure 2e-g). This suggests damage avoidance is more important than repair for survival.
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not explicitly challenge the statistical findings, they raised concerns about the underlying assumptions that would affect interpretation of these results. Essential Revision 1 notes concerns about 'over-conceptualization' and that 'the true relationship between frailty index and damage is unknown.' The validity of comparing damage versus repair effects depends on whether the measured 'repair' represents true biological processes or artifacts (Essential Revisions 2-3), which reviewers questioned extensively. Language in discussion and conclusions was requested to be 'tempered.'

results.result: The authors claim that most health deficits in the mouse frailty index can reverse either spontaneously or through interventions (supported by Supplementary file 1), though some deficits (cataracts, tumors, diarrhea, prolapses) rarely or never repair in their data.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 directly challenges this claim, stating 'I do not believe many of the deficits in the mouse index are reversible under normal physiologic conditions' and providing a list of deficits they consider 'not truly reversible' including 'alopecia, loss of fur color, loss of whiskers, tumors, kyphosis, hearing loss, cataracts, corneal capacity, vision loss, rectal prolapse, genital prolapse.' The reviewer notes that 'any reversal that was observed must be due to random measurement error' for these deficits. Reviewer #3 also requested 'more discussion on why deficits can be repaired, especially for some deficits which may seem to represent irreversible processes.'

results.result: The study reports that enalapril and voluntary exercise interventions in mice affect both damage and repair processes in sex-specific ways. Exercise strongly reduces FI curvature and stops damage acceleration in both sexes, while showing differential effects on repair rates (stopping decline in females, attenuating in males). Enalapril attenuates repair rate decline and reduces damage rates, with stronger effects in females.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these findings as a 'key achievement' and 'second key contribution' (DOI 10.7554/eLife.77632.sa0), with Reviewer #3 finding 'the result on sex differences in effects of interventions on robustness and resilience very interesting.' However, the validity of these intervention effects depends on the underlying validity of the damage/repair framework, which reviewers questioned. Essential Revision 4 notes 'additional conceptual issues are present in mouse models given typically shorter time scales' and requests 'additional details to support assumptions made in mouse models.' The interpretation of these results is thus uncertain pending resolution of fundamental methodological concerns.

results.result: In humans, household wealth is positively correlated with repair rates and negatively correlated with damage rates, with stronger effects at younger ages. Wealth effects on timescales are particularly strong for damage (robustness), with states remaining healthy longer at higher wealth levels, especially in females.
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not directly challenge these specific findings, Reviewer #1 cautioned about language, noting 'wealth is not an intervention' and 'wealth per se does not influence frailty as worded in methods. In these data wealth is a variable which is often associated with health outcomes.' Reviewer #3 requested statistics on follow-up times to contextualize these findings. The interpretation of wealth effects through the damage/repair framework is subject to the same conceptual concerns raised about the overall approach (Essential Revisions 1-2).

results.result: The study reports that both damage and repair processes operate over a broad range of timescales, from the shortest measurement intervals to organismal lifetimes, as shown by state-survival curves in Figure 5. Different health attributes exhibit different recovery times, and repair can occur long after damage originally occurred.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 expressed particular concern about Figure 5 models, stating 'I would be particularly concerned with how this would affect the models in figure 5' in the context of measurement error. They found 'the models in figure 5 somewhat difficult to interpret considering the extensive censoring' and requested 'plain language interpretation.' Essential Revision 3 notes that the validity of repair models and 'interpretation of Figure 5' would be challenged if only a subset of deficits truly contribute to repair while others irreversibly increase. The timescale findings depend critically on whether observed transitions represent true biological processes or measurement artifacts.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that measurement errors could contribute to both damage and repair rates but argue these errors are small for mice (supported by citations) and a sensitivity analysis pruning putative errors shows no qualitative changes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 directly challenges the adequacy of addressing measurement error, stating 'How do the authors account for the measurement error which is inherent to the individual components of the mouse frailty index, and how might this error affect their models?' They note that while 'the mouse frailty index is highly robust to these measurement errors' when used as a sum, 'breaking apart the index into its components compromises this robustness.' Essential Revision 2 explicitly requires that 'the issue of measurement error in individual components that switch from out-of-range to in-range or vice versa needs to be addressed.' The sensitivity analysis provided appears insufficient to address reviewers' concerns about the fundamental impact of measurement error on the damage/repair framework.

results.result: The authors acknowledge as a limitation that fast damage and repair dynamics occurring on timescales shorter than measurement intervals may be missed, and measurements can only be interpreted as net damage and net repair between observed timepoints.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 raised concerns about temporal assumptions, questioning whether time intervals 'up to 2 months which is 7-10% of a mouse lifespan' can be considered 'small' as assumed by the model, and asking authors to 'justify this assumption and/or discuss the implications.' Essential Revision 5 requests 'detailed total follow-up time/time-course in both animal and human data' to understand 'how many times deficits can be damaged/repaired within a given time or relative period of life.' The authors' acknowledgment of this limitation is appropriate, though reviewers indicate more discussion is needed.

results.result: The study defines damage rates as the probability of acquiring a new deficit per unit time and repair rates as the probability of repairing a deficit per unit time, representing organism-level measures of robustness and resilience. An advantage of using binarized variables is that both can be estimated using similar methods on the same data.
results.evaluation: Essential Revision 2 requires authors to 'distinguish biological processes from mechanical definitions in rationale and discussion,' indicating concern that the operational definitions may not correspond to biological reality. Reviewer #1 notes that 'repair' in the manuscript 'refers to a switch from out-of-range to a return to in-range for variables and cut-points that are not defined,' and Essential Revision 2 states 'variables and cutpoints must be detailed.' The methodological approach is acknowledged but its biological validity is questioned.

results.result: The study reports higher FI scores in females versus males in both mice and humans, consistent with prior literature. The effects of age on damage and repair are qualitatively similar between sexes, though interventions can have sex-specific effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these observations. Reviewer #1 noted a factual correction needed: 'Female humans live longer but female B6 mice usually live shorter,' but this does not challenge the FI or rate findings. The sex-specific intervention effects were noted as interesting by Reviewer #3. These descriptive findings appear accepted, though their interpretation through the damage/repair framework is subject to the broader conceptual concerns.

results.result: The study notes that traditional frailty measures like the FI are assembled from health state data at specific ages and do not separate dynamic damage and repair processes, though strong associations exist between frailty measures and adverse health outcomes. Previous modeling work did not separately measure damage and repair.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these background statements about existing frailty measures and prior work. These claims provide context and rationale for the study's approach. However, Essential Revision 1 notes that the authors should 'address in the manuscript rationale' the relationship between FI and damage, suggesting the rationale needs strengthening.

results.result: The study describes three mouse datasets with different assessment frequencies and interventions (enalapril, exercise), and one human dataset (ELSA) with specific inclusion criteria. The mouse frailty index comprises 31 (or 29) non-invasive health measures scored on defined scales, while the human FI uses 23 ADL/IADL items.
results.evaluation: Essential Revision 2 explicitly requires 'variables and cutpoints must be detailed,' and Essential Revision 3 requests authors 'include details on specific variables and their cutpoints' and 'indicate which of these variables change dynamically over time – with evidence of both 'deficit' and 'repair' – versus those that are irreparable by definition or thresholds.' Reviewer #1 notes 'I would also recommend the authors include a supplemental table with the specific mouse measurements and human questionnaire items.' While basic dataset descriptions are provided, reviewers indicate insufficient detail is given about the specific variables and their properties.

results.result: The study uses a joint modeling framework to model repair and damage rates while assessing their effect on survival in mice (but not humans, where mortality data were unavailable).
results.evaluation: Reviewer #3 noted an inconsistency in the text that should be corrected: 'This narrative should be changed then to reflect the fact that the joint model was only used in mice data.' This is a minor correction rather than a challenge to the approach. Essential Revision 6 raises 'concern over the impact of selection bias/survivor bias in models (especially mice)' and requests this be 'addressed in the model and discussion,' but does not reject the joint modeling approach itself.

Peer reviewers express uncertainty, raising fundamental concerns about the conceptual framework linking frailty index to damage and questioning whether observed 'repair' represents true biological processes or measurement error.
